home.memeSub: The fun stuff, front and center — because a whale-girl desktop pet is a legitimate productivity tool.
home.whatP1: DeepSeek Harness is the AI agent harness DeepSeek open-sourced on Aug 13, 2026 under the MIT license — the official README still labels it a developer preview. The name is a mouthful, so the community just says dsh, same as the npm package {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh.
home.whatP2: The whole idea fits in one line: everything is a plugin. The core is a tiny scheduler (the Cordis architecture) and the UI, tools, skins and desktop pets all plug into it — which is how a task board and a whale-girl pet ended up living in the same ecosystem.
home.whatP3: Want to see for yourself? One command — npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web — and the interface opens in your browser. First time here? Follow the install guide; it takes about five minutes.

skins.title: 🎨 DeepSeek Harness Skins & Themes
skins.sub: How do you change dsh skins? Every skin and theme plugin we've catalogued, sorted by stars — pick one, swap it in with a single command.
skins.whatH: What a skin is: how dsh theming works
skins.whatP1: DeepSeek Harness runs its interface as a web UI (the page that opens in your browser after the npx launch), and because everything is a plugin, a skin isn't a config flag — it is a plugin. Install it, enable it, and the interface changes; disable it to go back to the default, or stack several for a remix.
skins.whatP2: That's why the community's reskins run the whole spectrum: full whale-girl maid interfaces, a one-click Galgame-style conversation view, and small jobs like swapping the background or the status-label text. Different scale, same mechanism.
skins.howH: How to change your skin: three generic steps
skins.howP1: Step one: get dsh running — if you haven't installed it yet, the install guide takes about five minutes. Step two: pick a skin from the list below, open its page, copy the install command and paste it into your terminal. Step three: enable the plugin on the web UI's plugin page and refresh — new skin on.
skins.howP2: Two caveats: skin plugins may target different dsh versions, so skim the repo README first; and skins are community code too — for anything that deeply rewrites the UI, reading the code before installing is just good hygiene.

pets.cultureH: Pet culture: a week in, the whales came first

install.title: Install DSH
install.sub: From zero to running DeepSeek Harness, following the checkpoints: open a terminal, install Node.js, start dsh, then add a few community plugins. It takes about 5 minutes — no programming background required.
install.whatP: DeepSeek Harness is the agent framework DeepSeek open-sourced in August 2026. The community found the name a mouthful and just calls it dsh, same as the npm package {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh. Its whole idea is that everything is a plugin: the UI, tools and skins all plug into a small core.
install.needP: You need Node.js on your machine — both npx and pnpm work for starting it. Type node -v in your terminal; a version number means you are ready. If nothing prints, grab the LTS build from the Node.js website.
install.startP1: The easy way is one npx command: no global install, and it boots straight into the web UI.
install.startP2: If you've already installed Claude Code or Codex, it's the same idea — one npx command and you're in.
install.startP3: If you would rather read the source or hack on it, cloning the official repo works just as well.
install.pluginP: With DSH running, installing a plugin is still one command. Swap owner/repo below for the plugin you want, paste it into your terminal, then enable the plugin on the DSH Web UI plugin page. All {n} plugin pages in this hub carry a one-click copy button — no typing needed.

faq.q1: How do I install DeepSeek Harness?
faq.a1: Make sure Node.js is installed, run npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web in your terminal, and the web UI opens in your browser. Cloning the official repo and running it locally works too.
faq.q2: How do I install a DSH plugin?
faq.a2: Run dsh plugin add github:owner/repo in your terminal with owner/repo pointing at the plugin repo, then enable it on the web UI plugin page. Every plugin page in this hub has a one-click copy button for the exact command.
faq.a3: Honestly, they are community projects and quality varies. Spend two minutes reading the code before installing, and keep in mind that plugins can touch your API key, so skip repos you do not trust.
faq.q4: How do I submit my own plugin?
faq.a4: Use the Submit page of this site with your repo link — we review every submission by hand.
faq.q5: Are dsh and DeepSeek Harness the same thing?
faq.a5: Yes. DeepSeek Harness is the full name, dsh is what the community calls it, and the npm package is {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh.
faq.q6: The install fails, throws an error, or won't open — now what?
faq.a6: dsh is still a developer preview, so errors happen. The reliable move: copy the exact error text and search the official GitHub repo's Discussions first, then ask — chances are someone already hit the same wall. This site doesn't relay mystery "fixes" or make solutions up.
faq.q7: Does it work on Windows, macOS and Linux?
faq.a7: Yes. dsh is a Node.js program and works on all three desktop systems: PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS, whatever your Linux distro ships. Once Node.js v20+ is installed the commands are identical. Curious about phones? See the community Android project on the launchers page.

install.typoP: A fair share of visitors get here by typing it wrong. deepseekharness without the space, deepseek hardness with an extra d, deepseek herness missing an a — all point to the same project. The correct spelling is DeepSeek Harness, two words, dsh for short. The commands above work no matter how you spelled it.

about.title: About DSH Meme Hub
about.p1: On Aug 13, 2026, DeepSeek open-sourced DeepSeek Harness (dsh) with the slogan "Everything is a Plugin". 96k stars later, the dsh-plugin topic holds thousands of repositories — and somewhere between the file managers and the TDD frameworks, the community built whale-girl desktop pets, QQ2006 skins, and a knockoff web-game ad network for your terminal.
about.p2: Other directories list everything, with trust scores and manifest checks. We do something different: we pick the good stuff — and the fun stuff. Every entry here was looked at by a human, has a working install command, and the meme section only contains things that made us actually laugh.
about.p3: Data (stars, last push, license, manifest presence) is refreshed from the GitHub API. This site is a static, fully prerendered, multilingual (EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文 / DE) guide — fast on any connection.

compare.title: DeepSeek Harness vs Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode: Which Is Better?
compare.sub: Six common rivals — one overview table plus one section each. Publicly verifiable facts only; star counts and pricing change, so they're deliberately left out.
compare.introP: DeepSeek Harness — dsh to the community — is the agent harness DeepSeek open-sourced in August 2026 under the MIT license; the official README still labels it a developer preview. It gets compared to terminal agents like Claude Code and Codex, and there are community projects orbiting DeepSeek as well. This page covers positioning, vendor and open-source status, install method, and who each tool is for.

dshRow.pos: agent harness, everything is a plugin

cc.p1: Claude Code is Anthropic's closed-source, commercial terminal agent, tightly coupled to the Claude models. DeepSeek Harness is DeepSeek's own take: MIT-licensed and open, with a tiny core and the UI, tools and skins all plugged in via the Cordis architecture.
cc.p2: The ecosystems feel different too: Claude Code leans on Anthropic's commercial ecosystem and MCP extensions; dsh, young as it is, already counts 5000+ repositories under topic:dsh-plugin on GitHub with more arriving daily (see GitHub for current numbers), growing from productivity tools all the way to whale-girl pets. Both install in one line, so trying both costs you little.

codex.p1: Codex is OpenAI's closed-source, commercial coding agent — same terminal-plus-one-command school, tied to OpenAI's models and services.
codex.p2: The dsh difference is the same line again: MIT open source, everything is a plugin. Reading the source, patching the core or shipping your own plugin distribution is something closed tools can't offer. Do note it's still a developer preview — fast-moving and occasionally bumpy — so if you need rock-solid productivity today, watch it for a release or two.

opencode.p1: OpenCode is a community-built, open-source terminal agent. What it shares with dsh: open source, one-command startup, and no lock-in to a single commercial product.
opencode.p2: The difference is philosophy: OpenCode focuses on doing the terminal coding experience well; dsh makes "everything is a plugin" the selling point — pets and skins included — so its ecosystem grows wilder. Quiet terminal coding leans OpenCode; a house full of plugins leans dsh.

reasonix.p1: Reasonix is a community-built, DeepSeek-native terminal agent, open source on GitHub. It serves the same crowd as dsh — developers running agents on DeepSeek models — but the two have no official relationship.
reasonix.p2: Choosing between them is a matter of taste: the official harness with the everything-is-a-plugin ecosystem points to dsh; a lighter, independent project focused on the terminal agent itself is Reasonix's pitch. Both live on GitHub — ten minutes each tells you which fits your hand.

pi.p1: Pi agent is another community DeepSeek-native terminal agent, open source on GitHub, with no official ties to dsh.
pi.p2: It sits in the same spot as Reasonix: betting on the "terminal agent specialized for DeepSeek models" lane itself. For the plugin ecosystem and official backing pick dsh; for a light, independent tool, add it to the shortlist and try them side by side.

omnigent.p1: Omnigent is a meta-harness that orchestrates multiple agents — its layer is "how several agents work together". dsh works a different layer: inside one agent, everything is a plugin.
omnigent.p2: So this is less either-or than it looks, and the two can plausibly be combined (dsh is MIT-licensed — remix away). How exactly to wire them together is a question for each project's official docs, not for second-hand retellings, including this site's.

compare.pickH: How to choose: four honest lines
compare.pick1: Open source you control, plugin tinkering, a meme-friendly ecosystem — DeepSeek Harness. Start with the install guide.
compare.pick2: Your workflow is already welded to the Claude or OpenAI suite — stick with each vendor's own tool for now and revisit when dsh ships a stable release.
compare.pick3: You just don't want a terminal — hold off on choosing at all and look at the GUI launchers first; double-click and go.
compare.pick4: One last honest line: dsh is in beta. When something breaks, search or post in the official GitHub Discussions — that beats folk remedies.

faq.q1: DeepSeek Harness or Claude Code — which is better?
faq.a1: Neither wins outright: for open source, hackability and an exploding plugin ecosystem, dsh; for maturity inside the Claude ecosystem, Claude Code. dsh is still a developer preview — treat stability accordingly.
faq.a2: The framework itself is MIT-licensed and free. The model calls you make while running an agent are billed by whichever model service you use — that's separate from the license.
faq.q3: Are dsh, Reasonix and Pi agent related?
faq.a3: They all orbit DeepSeek but have no official relationship: dsh is DeepSeek's own harness; Reasonix and Pi agent are independent community terminal agents. Check each GitHub repo for the current state.
